questions.question_text:
Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = e^{3x^{2}}$.
Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Differentiated the index as well as bringing it down; the index stays $3x^{2}$.
Left out the inner derivative $6x$ required by the chain rule.
Multiplied by the index itself instead of by the derivative of the index.

questions.question_text:
Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = e^{1-4x^{3}}$.
Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Lost the negative sign when differentiating $1 - 4x^{3}$.
Replaced the index with its own derivative; the index must stay $1 - 4x^{3}$.
Reduced the power of $x$ without multiplying by the index $3$, giving $-4x^{2}$ instead of $-12x^{2}$.

questions.question_text:
Use the product rule to differentiate $y = xe^{5x}$.
Give your answer in factored form.

options.why: Multiplied the two derivatives together instead of using $u'v + uv'$.
Used $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{5x}\right) = e^{5x}$, omitting the factor $5$.
Kept only the $uv'$ term and dropped $u'v$.

questions.solution_text:
$y = xe^{5x}$
Product rule with $u = x$ and $v = e^{5x}$:
$y' = u'v + uv'$
$= 1\left(e^{5x}\right) + x\left(5e^{5x}\right)$
$= e^{5x}(1 + 5x)$

questions.question_text:
Use the quotient rule to differentiate $y = \dfrac{e^{4x}}{x+2}$.
Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Added instead of subtracted when combining $4x + 8 - 1$ in the numerator.
Used $\dfrac{uv' - u'v}{v^{2}}$, reversing the order of the two numerator terms.
Differentiated the numerator and the denominator separately instead of using the quotient rule.

questions.question_text:
Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = \left(e^{4x}-1\right)^{2}$.
Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Left out the inner derivative $4e^{4x}$ of the bracket.
Used $e^{4x}$ as the inner derivative instead of $4e^{4x}$.
Expanded $\left(e^{4x}-1\right)^{2}$ as $e^{8x}-1$, dropping the middle term.

questions.question_text:
Use the chain rule to differentiate $y = e^{x^{2}+7x}$.
Give your answer in simplest form.

options.why: Multiplied by the index itself instead of its derivative $2x+7$.
Left out the inner derivative $2x+7$ required by the chain rule.
Replaced the index with its derivative instead of leaving it unchanged.

questions.question_text: For $f(x) = e^{x^{2}-3x}$, find the exact value of $f'(3)$.

options.why: Evaluated $f(3) = e^{0} = 1$ instead of the derivative.
Used $2x = 6$ as the inner derivative, forgetting the $-3$ from $x^{2}-3x$.

questions.question_text: Differentiate $y = x^{2}e^{3x}$, giving your answer fully factored.

options.why: Used $e^{3x}$ instead of $3e^{3x}$ as the derivative of the exponential.
Kept only the $uv'$ term and omitted $u'v = 2xe^{3x}$.
Multiplied the derivatives $2x$ and $3e^{3x}$ instead of using $u'v + uv'$.

questions.solution_text:
$y = x^{2}e^{3x}$
Product rule with $u = x^{2}$ and $v = e^{3x}$:
$y' = u'v + uv'$
$= 2x\left(e^{3x}\right) + x^{2}\left(3e^{3x}\right)$
$= xe^{3x}(2 + 3x)$

options.why: Omits the derivative of the inner function $x^4$.
Changes the exponent and does not apply the chain rule correctly.
Puts the inner derivative in the exponent instead of multiplying by it.
Incorrectly applied the power rule to a variable exponent, multiplying by $3-0.2x$ and subtracting one from the exponent.
This omits the derivative of the exponent.
Replaced the exponent with its derivative $-0.2$ and omitted the multiplier $-0.2$ required by the chain rule.

questions.solution_text: For $e^{u}$, the derivative is $u'e^u$. With $u=3-0.2x$, $u'=-0.2$, giving $-0.2e^{3-0.2x}$.
